title: Merge Intervals
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated rescan-and-merge versus sorting by start time and merging in a single pass.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Merge all overlapping intervals\"","Sort by start time first; overlapping intervals become adjacent, so a single pass suffices"],["Combining ranges into their union","Extend the last merged interval's end whenever the next interval overlaps it"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Two intervals overlap if one starts before or when the other ends. Sorting by start time first ensures that if any interval overlaps another, it must overlap the interval immediately preceding it in this sorted order (or one already merged into a running interval), making a single left-to-right pass sufficient.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Overlapping Reservation Time Blocks
blocks.text: Picture several reservation time blocks for the same resource, some of which overlap and should be combined into a single continuous block. Sorting the reservations by start time first, then merging each into the CURRENT combined block if it overlaps (otherwise starting a new combined block), produces the final set of non-overlapping combined reservations in one pass.

blocks.caption: Sorting by start time makes overlapping intervals adjacent, enabling a single merging pass

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Result: [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]. [1,3] and [2,6] overlap and merge into [1,6]; [8,10] and [15,18] are separate.
5. How Should We Think?

Before repeatedly re-scanning for overlapping pairs, notice that sorting by start time first guarantees any overlap must occur between an interval and the one immediately preceding it (or the running merged interval), so a single pass suffices to merge everything correctly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If intervals are sorted by start time, and the current interval's start is less than or equal to the end of the LAST merged interval, they overlap (or touch) and should be combined.

Observation 2: Combining means extending the last merged interval's end to the maximum of its current end and the new interval's end, since the new interval might extend further right, or might be entirely contained within the existing merged range.

Observation 3: If the current interval does NOT overlap the last merged interval, it starts a brand new merged interval in the result.

Observation 4: A single left-to-right pass after sorting correctly produces every merged interval, since once sorted, no interval later in the sequence could possibly overlap an EARLIER merged interval without also overlapping the one immediately before it.
This leads to sorting intervals by start time, then a single pass: extend the last merged interval if the current one overlaps it, otherwise start a new merged interval.
6. Brute Force Solution
Repeatedly scan the list for any two overlapping intervals, merge them into one, and repeat until no more overlaps are found.
Step by step algorithm

items: Scan all pairs of intervals for any overlap.
If an overlapping pair is found, merge them into one combined interval and restart the scan.
Repeat until a full scan finds no more overlapping pairs.

codes.python:
def merge_intervals_brute(intervals):
    intervals = [list(iv) for iv in intervals]
    merged_something = True
    while merged_something:                              # repeat until no more merges happen
        merged_something = False
        for i in range(len(intervals)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(intervals)):
                a, b = intervals[i], intervals[j]
                if a[0] <= b[1] and b[0] <= a[1]:            # check overlap directly
                    a[0], a[1] = min(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1])
                    intervals.pop(j)
                    merged_something = True
                    break
            if merged_something:
                break
    return intervals

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly scanning and merging directly implements the "keep merging until nothing overlaps" definition.
Restarting the scan after every single merge is wasteful, potentially costing O(n cubed) in the worst case.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: up to O(n cubed) in the worst case, due to repeated full rescans after each merge.
Space: O(n) for the result.
Limitation: sorting by start time first means overlaps can only occur between adjacent (or running-merged) intervals, letting a SINGLE pass replace repeated rescanning, achieving O(n log n) instead.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why repeated rescanning is unnecessary: once sorted by start time, any overlap involving a given interval can ONLY be with the interval immediately before it (or the currently accumulating merged interval), never with something further back that has already been finalized.

The single-pass merge: maintain a result list; for each interval in sorted order, if it overlaps the LAST interval in the result (its start is <= that interval's end), extend that last interval's end; otherwise, append the current interval as a new entry.

Why this is correct: sorting guarantees that once an interval in the result list is "closed" (a later interval did not overlap it), no even-later interval could overlap it either, since starts only increase.

The core idea: sort once, then a single O(n) pass merging into the result list directly.
Sort intervals by start time. In a single pass, extend the last interval in the result if the current one overlaps it (start <= last end); otherwise append it as a new interval.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for intervals = [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]] (already sorted by start)

blocks.caption: A single pass after sorting merges each interval into the result directly

blocks.text: Why This Works

Sorting by start time guarantees that any interval overlapping a previously merged interval must overlap the LATEST such interval currently in the result, since all intervals between them (if any) have starts that fall in between and were already accounted for. This means checking only against the result's last entry, in a single forward pass, correctly and completely merges every overlapping group without ever needing to rescan.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the sort.
Space: O(n) for the result.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Merge Intervals is the foundational "sort by start, single pass merge" technique, reused throughout nearly every interval-related problem.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting to sort first, attempting to merge in the original (arbitrary) input order.
Using "<" instead of "<=" when checking overlap, incorrectly treating touching intervals (like [1,3] and [3,5]) as non-overlapping when the problem intends them to merge.

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "sort by start time, then a single pass since overlaps can only be with the most recent merged interval" demonstrates the key insight clearly before coding.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "merge all overlapping intervals", think: sort by start time, then a single pass extending or starting new merged intervals.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you adapt this for Insert Interval, where a single new interval is added to an already-sorted, already-merged list?
How would you handle streaming intervals that arrive over time, without re-sorting from scratch each time?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Insert Interval, Meeting Rooms, and Interval List Intersections, all building on this same sort-then-scan interval technique.
Any "combine overlapping ranges into their union" problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Repeated rescan-and-merge costs up to O(n cubed) time; sorting then a single pass costs O(n log n) time, both using O(n) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: sort by start time, then a single pass merging each interval into the result.
Core Idea: extend the last merged interval's end if the current interval overlaps it; otherwise, start a new merged interval.
Time: up to O(n cubed) for repeated rescanning, O(n log n) for sort-then-scan.
Most Important Observation: sorting by start time confines every possible overlap to be with the most recently merged interval, enabling a single pass.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, extremely frequently reused interval technique.
One line memory trick: sort by start; extend the last merged interval if it overlaps, else start fresh.
